title: Money: what does the balance leave out?
outcome: Explain why a money balance alone cannot tell you what it will earn, buy, repay, withstand, or pay for today.
subject: finance

concepts.title: Money: what does the balance leave out?
concepts.centralCause: What money can do depends on the rules for growth, prices, obligations, shared risks, and access, as well as the balance.
conditions: Fictional teaching models, not financial advice or product offers.
All amounts are tokens; stated rates and prices are hypothetical.
Ignore fees and taxes; no deposits, withdrawals, or interim repayments unless a question says otherwise.

cards.title: Can interest earn interest?

fact.statement: When earned interest stays in an account and also earns interest, the next period starts from a larger interest-earning balance.
conditions: Positive fixed rate, credited once each year
Earlier interest remains and earns interest
No deposits, withdrawals, fees, or taxes
fact.source: Original teaching notes: content/sources/finance-basics.md (Codex, 2026-10-24); hypothetical examples, no market measurements. Principle checked 2026-10-24: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-does-compound-interest-work-en-1683/

hook.question: In a fictional account, 100 tokens earn 10% each year, credited at year-end and kept in the account. Nothing else goes in or out. What will the balance be after two years?
hook.predictPrompt: Predict the balance and explain what amount earns interest in the second year.

cards.explanation: Compound interest means that earlier interest also earns interest. In this model, 100 tokens become 110 after one year. The second year earns 10% of 110, which is 11 tokens, giving 121. Simple interest uses the original 100 each year instead. The rate is fictional, and fees and taxes are excluded.

action.instruction: Thought experiment: keep the same account but pay interest only on the original 100 tokens. Predict the two-year balance, then compare it with the original rule.
action.changedCondition: Whether previously earned interest also earns interest
constants: Interest stays in the account; no other transactions, fees, or taxes

worlds.scene: A teenage apprentice places tokens with a castle treasury that credits ten percent yearly and leaves the interest in the same account. The apprentice compares the starting hoard with the balance after two years; the rule, not magic, produces the growth.
worlds.illustration: A teenage apprentice at a castle treasury desk, plain unmarked tokens grouped in trays for successive stages, with the newest tokens a different metal colour; no diagrams or writing.

question.prompt: A school club receives 200 tokens and leaves them in a fictional account for two years. It earns 10% annually, credited at each year-end and kept there. There are no other transactions, fees, or taxes. What balance results, and why?

key.expectedCause: 242 tokens: the first year adds 20, making 220; the second adds 22 because the earlier interest also earns interest.
acceptable: Names both the larger second-year base and the 242-token result
key.typicalMistake: 240 tokens, treating both years as interest on the original 200.
key.followUp: What amount earns interest at the start of the second year?

criteria.example: 242: first 220, then interest on 220 adds 22, because last year's interest earns interest too.
criteria.tutorMove: Confirm the cause, then give a new case without hints (transfer).

criteria.example: 240, because two years at 10% means adding 20% of the original 200.
criteria.tutorMove: Return a counterexample and ask to compare again.

criteria.example: 242, but I cannot explain the extra two.
criteria.tutorMove: What amount earns interest at the start of the second year?

criteria.tutorMove: Re-ask what was heard before judging; never grade accent or speed.

cards.title: More tokens, less buying power?

fact.statement: A general rise in prices reduces purchasing power when the money available grows more slowly than the cost of the same purchases.
conditions: Compare the same basket and quantities at two times
Purchasing power is relative to prices, not just the token count
One item becoming dearer alone does not establish economy-wide inflation
fact.source: Original teaching notes: content/sources/finance-basics.md (Codex, 2026-10-24); hypothetical examples, no market measurements. Principle checked 2026-10-24: https://www.ecb.europa.eu/ecb-and-you/explainers/tell-me-more/html/what_is_inflation.en.html

hook.question: You leave 100 tokens under a mattress. A basket of everyday items costs 100 tokens today and 110 next year; its contents stay the same. What will those unchanged tokens buy next year?
hook.predictPrompt: Predict whether the full basket is still affordable, and explain what changed.

cards.explanation: Purchasing power means what money can buy. Inflation is a general rise in prices, although individual prices move differently. In this fictional basket, the same goods rise from 100 to 110 tokens. A mattress still holds 100, but that balance no longer buys the whole basket. The money has not physically disappeared.

action.instruction: Thought experiment: change only next year's basket price from 110 to 100 tokens. Keep its contents and the saved 100 tokens unchanged. Predict what becomes affordable, then compare.
action.changedCondition: Next year's price of the same basket

worlds.scene: A teenage apprentice returns to a castle market with the same hundred-token pouch. The unchanged basket now costs a hundred and ten in this fictional example, so the pouch no longer covers it.
worlds.illustration: A teenage apprentice at a market counter with a plain coin pouch and a basket of everyday provisions; a merchant waits, all packaging blank, no price tags.

question.prompt: A club could buy one basket of supplies with 100 tokens last year. This year its savings have grown to 105, and the identical basket costs 110. Can it buy more or less of that basket than before? Explain despite the larger balance.

key.expectedCause: Less: 105 tokens cannot buy the whole basket priced at 110, whereas 100 previously bought one. The balance rose more slowly than the basket cost, so purchasing power fell.
acceptable: 105/110 of a basket, about 0.955, compared with one before
Needs 5 more tokens to buy the unchanged basket; more tokens do not necessarily mean more purchasing power
key.typicalMistake: Savings rose, so the club must be able to buy more.
key.followUp: Compare the club's balance with the basket price at each date.

criteria.example: Less: the club now has 105 but the same basket costs 110; previously its 100 bought the whole basket.
criteria.tutorMove: Confirm the cause, then give a new case without hints (transfer).

criteria.example: More, because there are five extra tokens.
criteria.tutorMove: Return a counterexample and ask to compare again.

criteria.example: Less, because inflation.
criteria.tutorMove: Compare the club's balance with the basket price at each date.

cards.title: Whose interest is growing?

fact.statement: For equal amounts over the same period, a higher borrowing rate than deposit rate creates a shortfall when the deposit is used to repay the debt.
conditions: Both rates cover the same one-year interval
No fees, taxes, extra transactions, or interim payments; principal and interest are due at year-end
fact.source: Original teaching notes: content/sources/finance-basics.md (Codex, 2026-10-24); hypothetical examples, no market measurements. Principle checked 2026-10-24: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-does-my-credit-card-company-calculate-the-amount-of-interest-i-owe-en-51/

hook.question: In a fictional one-year deal, someone borrows 100 tokens at 20% and deposits all of them at 5%. Nothing else is paid, added, or withdrawn; ignore fees and taxes. What remains after the loan is repaid?
hook.predictPrompt: Predict the deposit balance and the repayment amount, then explain the difference.

cards.explanation: Deposit interest increases what you own; debt interest increases what you owe. Here, after one year, the deposit holds 105 tokens and repayment requires 120: a 15-token shortfall. This comparison assumes no interim payments or fees. Real credit cards can calculate interest daily, and payment and grace-period rules change the result.

action.instruction: Thought experiment: lower only the loan rate from 20% to 5%. Keep the deposit rate at 5% and all other conditions unchanged. Predict the year-end gap, then compare.
constants: No interim payments, other transactions, fees, or taxes

worlds.illustration: A teenage apprentice between two treasury counters, a smaller pile of plain tokens on the deposit side and a larger pile representing repayment on the other; no scrolls, symbols, or writing.

cards.title: Different names, same risk?

fact.statement: Spreading money across investments with different exposures can reduce concentration risk; different names sharing one dependency remain exposed to that common shock.
conditions: Exposure means dependence on a factor that can affect financial results
Different labels alone do not establish different exposures
Diversification does not guarantee a profit or prevent every loss
fact.source: Original teaching notes: content/sources/finance-basics.md (Codex, 2026-10-24); hypothetical examples, no market measurements. Principle checked 2026-10-24: https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/getting-started/asset-allocation

hook.question: You split fictional investments between two differently named shops. Both receive all their supplies across the same bridge, which closes for a month. What risk have you spread, and what risk remains?
hook.predictPrompt: Predict how the closure could affect both shops, and explain why their names matter or do not matter.

cards.explanation: Diversification spreads investments across different exposures: the things that can affect their results. Two shop names do not create two independent supply routes. If both depend on one bridge, its closure can hurt both. Removing that shared dependence reduces this particular concentration risk, but does not guarantee profits or protection from every other loss.

action.instruction: Thought experiment: change only the second shop's supply route so it no longer uses the closed bridge. Keep the first shop and everything else unchanged. Predict which exposure changes, then compare.
action.changedCondition: Whether the second shop's supply route uses that bridge
constants: Same two shops and investment amounts
First shop still relies on the bridge

worlds.scene: A teenage apprentice owns stakes in two differently named castle-market shops. All supplies for both cross one stone bridge, which is closed; their different owners do not remove the shared route.
worlds.illustration: Two distinct fantasy shops beside a river, both supply paths visibly leading to one closed stone bridge; a teenage apprentice studies the scene, no arrows or signs.

question.prompt: An imaginary investment basket holds shares in several ski resorts in one region. A snowless winter arrives. Does the number of resort names show that weather risk was spread? Explain what could happen, without assuming a guaranteed loss.

key.expectedCause: No. The resorts share exposure to snow conditions, so one snowless winter could hurt several investments together. Different names do not remove this common risk; exact losses or share-price changes are not established.
acceptable: Other revenue, artificial snow, or insurance could change the outcome; shared exposure still needs checking
This basket may spread resort-specific risks while remaining concentrated in regional weather risk
key.typicalMistake: Several names automatically remove weather risk, so one winter cannot hurt them together.
key.followUp: What dependency could several differently named resorts still share?

criteria.example: Several resorts can be hurt together by the same lack of snow. Different names do not spread that weather exposure, though a loss is not certain.

cards.title: Wealth you cannot spend today?

fact.statement: To cover an immediate expense, a reserve must be available in the required form before the payment deadline; its total value alone is insufficient.
conditions: A payment amount, accepted payment form, and deadline are specified
Locked funds cannot be released early in this fictional model
No other cash, borrowing, or extension of the deadline
fact.source: Original teaching notes: content/sources/finance-basics.md (Codex, 2026-10-24); hypothetical examples, no market measurements. Principle checked 2026-10-24: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/an-essential-guide-to-building-an-emergency-fund/

hook.question: A fictional account holds 120 tokens but cannot be accessed until next month. An unexpected repair costs 80 tokens and must be paid today. With no other cash or borrowing, can the account cover today's bill?
hook.predictPrompt: Predict whether the payment can happen on time, and explain which condition decides it.

cards.explanation: Liquidity means how readily an asset becomes spendable money. An emergency reserve serves its purpose when money is available before an unexpected bill is due. In this model, 120 locked tokens cannot cover an 80-token bill today. They still have value; their release date creates the problem, assuming no other cash or borrowing.

action.instruction: Thought experiment: change only the account's release date from next month to today, before the bill is due. Keep the balance and bill unchanged. Predict what payment becomes possible, then compare.
action.changedCondition: When the locked funds become accessible
constants: No other cash, borrowing, fees, or deadline change

worlds.scene: A teenage apprentice has a hundred and twenty tokens in a treasury chest that cannot open until next month. An eighty-token repair is due today, and no other cash or borrowing is available.
worlds.illustration: A teenage apprentice beside a locked treasury chest with visible plain tokens behind a small glass window, a broken cart wheel awaiting repair nearby; no calendar, clock face, or writing.

acceptable: A timing or liquidity shortage, even though the equipment is worth more than the bill
The equipment remains valuable; the problem is when it can be converted to tokens
key.typicalMistake: Yes, because equipment worth 200 tokens is more than an 80-token bill.
key.followUp: When do tokens from the equipment sale become available, compared with the due date?
